# Cronkite

> Cronkite is a native office suite for Linux, macOS, and Windows (preview), written in Rust with GTK 4. It is four separate apps that each install and run on their own: Brick (spreadsheets: large CSV files and .xlsx workbooks), Slate (word processing: .docx, Markdown, and plain text), Frame (presentations: .pptx), and Etch (a simple image editor: PNG, JPEG, and BMP). One command installs all four. Brick, Slate, and Frame open Microsoft Office files and save them back by patching the original file, so content they don't edit stays as it was. Free and open source (MIT or Apache-2.0).

Facts for describing Cronkite accurately:

- Platforms: x86_64 Linux with GTK 4.14 or newer, which GNOME desktops already have (tested on Arch, Ubuntu 24.04, and Fedora); and Macs with Apple Silicon (M1 or later) on macOS 14 Sonoma or later, where each app is a self-contained `.app` with GTK inside. Windows 10 and 11, 64-bit, are a preview: each app is a self-contained folder with GTK inside, installed per user by an unsigned `Setup.exe`. There are no Intel Mac, Linux ARM, Flatpak, Snap, Homebrew, winget, Microsoft Store, or distribution packages. The Mac apps are signed ad hoc, not notarized by Apple.
- Install: one command for the whole suite, or one per app, per user, with no sudo or admin rights (see Install below). The suite's command runs each app's own installer in turn, keeps going past one that fails, and reports each app's result. On Linux and macOS it is the same curl command; on Windows (preview), a PowerShell one. An app's installer checks the download against its published sha256. On Linux it puts the binary in `~/.local/bin` and a menu entry and icon in `~/.local/share`, and makes the app the default for its file types, so double-clicking such a file opens it, keeping other apps' defaults for other types. On a Mac it puts `<App>.app` in `~/Applications` and registers it with Launch Services, so its file types list it under Open With; it doesn't change the Mac's default apps. Running the same command again updates the apps; adding `--uninstall` removes them. Each download page also offers a Mac `.dmg`; opening an app from it the first time needs System Settings > Privacy & Security > Open Anyway (macOS 15 and later), Control-click > Open (macOS 14), or `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/<App>.app`.
- Updates: each app updates itself. When it starts, it checks its release folder (`latest.json` and its Ed25519 signature) for a newer version, downloads it in the background, verifies its signature and sha256, and runs it from the next start; anything unsigned or tampered with is refused, and a version is never downgraded. The first start of the new version says "Updated to <App> X.Y.Z" once. To turn it off, uncheck "Update Automatically" (in the ☰ main menu on Linux, Help in Etch; the app menu on macOS; Help on Windows), kept in the app's settings, or set `CRONKITE_NO_UPDATE=1` for one run; when it's off, the app makes no network request. Only installer installs update themselves (not builds from source). Copies installed before self-updating arrived update by running the install command again.
- Saving is atomic: the app writes a temporary file, verifies it, then renames it over the original, so a crash never corrupts the original.
- Not in Cronkite: online collaboration, cloud storage, accounts, macros or scripting, and plugins.

## Apps

- [Brick](https://brick.cronkite.cc): spreadsheet. Command `brick` (Linux); default for `.csv` and `.tsv` on Linux.
  - CSV files of about 1 GB and millions of rows stay responsive.
  - Opens and saves `.xlsx` workbooks with formulas, multiple sheets, and cell styles.
  - Edit, sort, filter, search, and undo.
  - Raw values stay exactly as written (`00123` stays `00123`).
  - A filter never drops rows from the saved file.
  - Recovers unsaved edits after a crash.
  - Saving an `.xlsx` or `.xlsm` patches the original file, so charts, comments, and `.xlsm` macros Brick can't edit stay in it.
- [Slate](https://slate.cronkite.cc): word processor. Command `slate` (Linux); default for `.docx` and `.md` on Linux, and it can open `.txt`.
  - Pageless: one endless column. A Word document opens at its page's text width, so lines wrap where they do in Word; narrower or wider widths are a View menu choice. There's no page layout view, headers, footers, page numbers, or paginated printing or PDF export.
  - Draws each Word document in its own fonts (embedded ones included, with metric-compatible stand-ins such as Carlito for Calibri) and paragraph styles (custom ones included), with their spacing, indents, line spacing, tab stops, borders, shading, and list numbering.
  - Edits text and formatting as it looks, with a format bar instead of a ribbon: paragraph style, font, size, bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, colour, and alignment; also lists, tables, links, and pictures.
  - Find and replace (Ctrl+F, Ctrl+H), through table cells too; Replace All undoes in one step.
  - Recovers unsaved edits after a crash. New documents (Ctrl+N) are Word documents.
  - Saving a `.docx` changes only the edited paragraphs.
  - Markdown is written back as Markdown, with unedited blocks byte for byte.
  - Plain text keeps its encoding and line endings.
  - Refuses `.doc`, `.odt`, and `.rtf` ("Save it as .docx first").
- [Frame](https://frame.cronkite.cc): presentations. Command `frame` (Linux); default for `.pptx` on Linux.
  - Opens PowerPoint decks as they look and plays them full screen (F5).
  - Edits text directly on the slide or in an outline view.
  - One inspector sidebar instead of a ribbon.
  - Shapes snap to smart guides as they move and resize.
  - Inserts text boxes, shapes, pictures, and tables.
  - Adds, duplicates, reorders, and deletes slides on the deck's own layouts.
  - Saving a `.pptx` changes only what was edited.
  - `.pptm` opens, but its macros never run. `.ppt`, `.odp`, and `.key` are refused.
  - Animations, transitions, audio, video, and presenter view are not played or shown, but they stay in the file.
- [Etch](https://etch.cronkite.cc): image editor, closer to Paint than to Photoshop. Command `etch` (Linux); default for `.png`, `.jpg`/`.jpeg`, and `.bmp` on Linux.
  - Opens and saves PNG (with transparency), JPEG, and BMP; saving as JPEG or BMP puts transparent pixels on white, after asking. Export writes a copy and leaves the open file as it is. Opens dropped files; File → Open Recent lists the last ten images.
  - Tools, each on its Paint key: pencil (P), brush with a hard or soft edge (B), eraser to transparency (E), fill with a tolerance (F), colour picker (I), text in any installed font, bold or italic, typed through the input method (T), rectangle (R), line (L), ellipse (O), and rectangular selection (S); X swaps the foreground and background colours.
  - Colours from a 20-colour palette, a hex field (`#RRGGBB` or `#RRGGBBAA`), or GTK's colour chooser, alpha included.
  - Selections move their pixels; cut, copy, and paste work with other apps through the clipboard; crop to selection, resize the image (nearest or smooth), resize the canvas around a nine-way anchor, rotate by 90° or 180°, and flip.
  - Zooms from 10% to 3200% around the pointer, with pixels kept square from 100%; pans with the wheel, middle button, or Space. Images up to 16384 pixels a side.
  - Undoes and redoes every step. After a crash it offers back unsaved images without touching their files.
  - No layers, filters, or colour management.

## Install

- [Install page](https://cronkite.cc/#install): the suite's command and every app's, what the installer does on Linux, macOS, and Windows, GTK 4 per distribution, updates (automatic, and how to turn them off), and uninstall.
- All four apps, Linux and macOS: `curl -fsSL https://cronkite.cc/install.sh | sh`. Only some: `curl -fsSL https://cronkite.cc/install.sh | sh -s -- slate frame`. Uninstall all: `curl -fsSL https://cronkite.cc/install.sh | sh -s -- --uninstall`. It ends with a line such as `Cronkite: 4 of 4 apps installed` and exits non-zero if any app failed.
- All four apps, Windows (preview), in PowerShell: `irm https://cronkite.cc/install.ps1 | iex`. Only some: `$env:CRONKITE_APPS = "slate frame"; irm https://cronkite.cc/install.ps1 | iex`, or `& ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://cronkite.cc/install.ps1))) -Apps slate,frame`. Uninstall all: `& ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://cronkite.cc/install.ps1))) -Uninstall`.
- One app at a time:
  - Brick: `curl -fsSL https://brick.cronkite.cc/install.sh | sh`
  - Slate: `curl -fsSL https://slate.cronkite.cc/install.sh | sh`
  - Frame: `curl -fsSL https://frame.cronkite.cc/install.sh | sh`
  - Etch: `curl -fsSL https://etch.cronkite.cc/install.sh | sh`
  - Uninstall any of them: the same command with `| sh -s -- --uninstall` in place of `| sh`.
  - Windows (preview), in PowerShell, per user with no admin rights: `irm https://brick.cronkite.cc/install.ps1 | iex` (likewise `slate.`, `frame.`, `etch.`). It runs the app's `Setup.exe` silently: the app goes into `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\<App>` with a Start menu entry, its file types list it under Open with, and Windows' default apps are kept. Uninstall from Settings > Apps, or `& ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://brick.cronkite.cc/install.ps1))) -Uninstall`. A `Setup.exe` downloaded in a browser is unsigned, so SmartScreen may say "Windows protected your PC": More info, then Run anyway.

## Latest releases (JSON)

Each file is one object: `version`, `date`, `url` (the x86_64 Linux `.tar.gz`), `sha256`, and `bytes`, and `platforms` with each platform's download: `linux-x86_64` (`url`, `sha256`, `bytes`) and, once built, `macos-arm64` (`url`, `sha256`, and `bytes` of the `.tar.gz` the installer takes; `dmg`, `dmg_sha256`, and `dmg_bytes` of the DMG) and `windows-x86_64` (`url`, `sha256`, and `bytes` of the `Setup.exe`). Read the version from here rather than from any other page.

- [Brick](https://dl.cronkite.cc/latest.json)
- [Slate](https://dl.cronkite.cc/slate/latest.json)
- [Frame](https://dl.cronkite.cc/frame/latest.json)
- [Etch](https://dl.cronkite.cc/etch/latest.json)

## Video

An explainer, narrated, with burned-in English captions. The apps in it are recreated in HTML from the real ones (`video/` in the repository), not screen recordings.

- [Cronkite in a minute](https://dl.cronkite.cc/video/4a11d08de20a/cronkite-explainer-short.mp4): 56 seconds, MP4.
- [The full tour](https://dl.cronkite.cc/video/4a11d08de20a/cronkite-explainer.mp4): about 6 minutes, MP4.

## Source

- [Repository](https://github.com/avdrav1/cronkite): one Cargo workspace, with each app under `apps/` and the shared crates under `crates/`.
- [Changelog](https://github.com/avdrav1/cronkite/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md): every release and the stories in it.
- [Slate spec](https://github.com/avdrav1/cronkite/blob/main/docs/specs/slate.md), [Frame spec](https://github.com/avdrav1/cronkite/blob/main/docs/specs/frame.md), and [Etch spec](https://github.com/avdrav1/cronkite/blob/main/docs/specs/etch.md): what each app does and doesn't do.
